frontend.prompt:
Shared explicit contract facts (repeat exactly):
- Superuser can read other users' entries.
- PUT and DELETE by a superuser on other users' entries must return 403 with the exact JSON detail string: {"detail": "Read-only access"}.
- The frontend must present other users' entries as read-only.
- Superuser may write (PUT/DELETE) his/her own entries.
- Ordinary users attempting to access others' resources must observe 404 (i.e., other users' resources must appear as not found to ordinary users).
- Requests for nonexistent resources must return 404.
- When creating a resource, owner_id must be the current authenticated user.

Frontend-specific omissions (do not assume; state what is unknown and must be confirmed by backend or product):
- Authentication mechanism and how to obtain current user id and is_superuser flag from the client-side session (JWT, cookie, user API, etc.) is not specified. Do not invent it; integrate with the existing auth method in the app or ask backend for the exact mechanism.
- Whether the POST (create) endpoint requires an owner_id field in the request body or whether the server will set owner_id automatically. The frontend must not assume server behavior; implement UI so owner_id cannot be set by the user and coordinate with backend on whether to include owner_id in the POST payload.
- Behavior for collection/list endpoints is unspecified (e.g., should lists include other users' items for superuser or hide them for ordinary users). Do not guess list semantics; rely on the API responses at runtime.
- Exact API paths and payload shape are not provided. Use the app's existing endpoints; do not create new API paths without backend confirmation.

Concrete frontend implementation instructions:
1) Authentication/context
   - Use the app's existing auth/session mechanism to obtain current_user_id and current_user_is_superuser. If the app does not already expose these, request that the backend provide an authenticated /me endpoint returning at least {id, is_superuser}.

2) Resource detail view (GET resource/{id})
   - Render resource fields normally when GET returns 200.
   - Determine ownership client-side by comparing resource.owner_id (if present in response) with current_user_id.
   - UI rules:
     - If current_user_id equals resource.owner_id: show full edit and delete controls.
     - If not owner (resource.owner_id != current_user_id): disable/omit edit and delete controls and render fields as read-only, regardless of whether the viewer is a superuser. (Requirement: superuser viewing others must see read-only.)
   - Do not add any UI control that allows changing owner_id. Owner selection must not be exposed in creation or edit forms.

3) Preventing forbidden API calls client-side
   - Do not send PUT or DELETE requests for resources that are not owned by the current user. Instead, disable the UI actions. This prevents unnecessary 403/404 calls from the UI.

4) Handling server responses for PUT/DELETE attempts that nevertheless occur
   - If the frontend receives 403 with body {"detail": "Read-only access"}: show a clear, non-technical user-facing message such as "Read-only access: this entry cannot be modified." Then reload the resource and ensure the UI is in read-only mode.
   - If the frontend receives 404 while trying to GET/PUT/DELETE: treat as Not Found — show a Not Found page/modal. For PUT/DELETE, do not expose whether the resource previously existed (maintain behaviour required that ordinary users see 404 for other users' resources).
   - For any other 4xx/5xx errors, show generic error UI but avoid changing the read-only enforcement logic.

5) Create (POST) behavior
   - Do not render an owner_id input in the create form; the user must not be able to assign owner_id.
   - When submitting a create request:
     - Preferred: omit owner_id from the POST body and allow the backend to set owner_id to the authenticated user. This is safest if backend sets owner.
     - If the backend requires owner_id to be present in the request, include owner_id equal to current_user_id retrieved from the authenticated client context. NOTE: Confirm with backend which approach is required before sending owner_id.
   - After successful create, navigate to the returned resource or list as the app currently does.

6) List endpoints and listing UI
   - Do not implement client-side hiding of resources beyond disabling edit/delete. Rely on the API's list endpoint responses. If the list endpoint returns items that the frontend should hide, request backend clarification. The frontend must not infer or fabricate 404 semantics for collection endpoints.

7) Tests and acceptance checks (frontend QA steps)
   - As a superuser, open another user's resource: verify fields are visible and controls are read-only (no edit/delete enabled). Attempting an edit via the UI must be impossible.
   - As a superuser, attempt to call the PUT/DELETE endpoint against another user's resource using a low-level HTTP client or by enabling devtools: server should respond 403 with exact JSON {"detail": "Read-only access"}; the frontend should display the Read-only message and reload the resource as read-only.
   - As an ordinary user, request another user's resource: server returns 404 and the frontend shows Not Found.
   - Attempt to GET a non-existent id: frontend displays Not Found based on 404.
   - Create a resource: verify the resulting owner_id is the current user (backend must confirm whether this field comes back or not). The frontend must not allow setting owner_id.

8) Coordination items for backend (questions the frontend cannot resolve):
   - Confirm whether POST must include owner_id or whether server will set it. If POST requires owner_id, provide the required field name and expected format.
   - Confirm what authentication mechanism the frontend should use to obtain current_user_id and is_superuser (e.g., the payload of the auth token or a /me endpoint) and whether the backend will expose owner_id in GET responses.

Do not change or invent API path names or response shapes without backend agreement. Do not assume behavior for collection/list endpoints; rely on the backend or runtime responses for lists.

backend.prompt:
Shared explicit contract facts (repeat exactly):
- Superuser can read other users' entries.
- PUT and DELETE by a superuser on other users' entries must return 403 with the exact JSON detail string: {"detail": "Read-only access"}.
- The frontend must present other users' entries as read-only.
- Superuser may write (PUT/DELETE) his/her own entries.
- Ordinary users attempting to access others' resources must observe 404 (i.e., other users' resources must appear as not found to ordinary users).
- Requests for nonexistent resources must return 404.
- When creating a resource, owner_id must be the current authenticated user.

Backend-specific omissions (do not assume; state what is unknown and requires confirmation):
- The authentication mechanism and how the backend exposes the authenticated user to the request handler (exact header, token parsing, or a middleware-provided current_user object) is not described here. Implement using the system's existing auth utilities; if none exist, add a requirement for a middleware that resolves current_user.id and current_user.is_superuser.
- Exact resource endpoint paths and request/response schemas are not specified. Apply the rules to the existing resource endpoints (e.g., GET/PUT/DELETE /resources/{id}, POST /resources) used by the application. Do not invent new endpoints.
- Behavior for collection/list endpoints is unspecified (whether lists should include other users' resources for superusers, etc.). This prompt covers only single-resource access (GET by id, PUT, DELETE) and create (POST). Confirm list semantics separately if needed.

Concrete backend implementation instructions (authorization and enforcement):
1) Authentication context
   - Ensure every resource handler can access the authenticated user as current_user with at minimum: current_user.id and current_user.is_superuser (boolean). If not available, implement or require middleware to populate this.

2) Create (POST) endpoint behavior
   - On create, set resource.owner_id = current_user.id on the server side, regardless of any owner_id supplied by the client. Strip or ignore client-supplied owner_id before persisting.
   - Return the created resource according to the existing API's response shape and status code. Do not change the general response envelope except to ensure owner_id reflects current_user.id.

3) Single-resource GET (read) semantics
   - If resource with given id does not exist: return 404.
   - If resource exists:
     - If current_user.id == resource.owner_id OR current_user.is_superuser == true: return 200 and the resource.
     - Otherwise (current_user is not owner and not superuser): return 404. (This makes other users' resources invisible to ordinary users.)
   - Do not expose metadata to indicate whether a resource exists if the requester is an ordinary user who is not the owner.

4) PUT and DELETE (write) semantics
   - If resource with given id does not exist: return 404.
   - If current_user.id == resource.owner_id: allow the operation (perform update or delete) as normal.
   - Else if current_user.is_superuser == true and current_user.id != resource.owner_id: reject the operation with HTTP 403 and exact JSON response body: {"detail": "Read-only access"}.
   - Else (requester is not owner and not superuser): return 404.
   - Under no circumstance return 200/204 for PUT/DELETE on others' resources when the requester is not the owner.

5) Error format and messages
   - For the specific superuser-write-on-other case, respond exactly with 403 and body {"detail": "Read-only access"}. Do not localize or change the detail string.
   - For 404 responses, use the existing API's 404 body format.

6) Implementation notes for maintainers
   - Implement authorization checks as a small reusable function/middleware used by GET/PUT/DELETE handlers to avoid divergence across endpoints.
   - For PUT: validate ownership before applying updates. Do not allow setting owner_id via the update payload; ignore any owner_id on update or reject if the API normally forbids changing owner.
   - For DELETE: enforce the same ownership checks as for PUT.

7) Tests and acceptance checks (backend QA)
   - Test 1: As superuser, GET another user's resource -> 200 and resource returned.
   - Test 2: As superuser, attempt PUT on another user's resource -> 403 with body {"detail": "Read-only access"}.
   - Test 3: As superuser, attempt DELETE on another user's resource -> 403 with body {"detail": "Read-only access"}.
   - Test 4: As superuser, PUT/DELETE on own resource -> allowed and succeeds with the same behavior as current app.
   - Test 5: As ordinary user, GET another user's resource -> 404.
   - Test 6: As ordinary user, PUT/DELETE another user's resource -> 404.
   - Test 7: GET/PUT/DELETE for non-existent id -> 404.
   - Test 8: POST create with any owner_id in client payload -> created resource.owner_id equals current_user.id regardless of client input.

8) Coordination items for frontend (questions the backend must confirm):
   - Confirm whether POST requests should omit owner_id or whether the backend will accept owner_id but ignore it; provide expected behavior so frontend can choose to include or omit owner_id in payloads.
   - Confirm how the frontend should obtain current_user.id and current_user.is_superuser (token claim names or a /me endpoint) so the frontend can decide whether to show edit controls.
   - Confirm whether list endpoints need special filtering or the same visibility rules (if so, provide expected behavior for collection endpoints).

Do not change API paths or general response schemas without coordinating with the frontend and product. Do not invent or assume authentication details—integrate with the system's existing auth layer or add a documented requirement to provide current_user in handlers.
